title: Round-Robin Load Balancer TOCTOU Race Causes Out-of-Bounds Panic
description: The LoadBalanceRoundRobin::get_ptr() method contains a time-of-check-time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition between the load of the current pointer value and the subsequent fetch_add or fetch_and. Two concurrent requests can both observe current_ptr at (num_upstreams - 2), both take the fetch_add(1) branch, and the second thread increments the pointer to num_upstreams, which is a valid but out-of-range index. The returned ptr value from fetch_add is the value *before* the increment, so the first caller gets (num_upstreams-2), and the second caller gets (num_upstreams-1). However, a third concurrent call could see current_ptr == num_upstreams (because the second call incremented past num_upstreams-1). It would then take the fetch_and(0) branch and return the stale value num_upstreams as ptr. This value is then used directly as an index into the upstream Vec, causing a panic on Vec::get() returning None, followed by an unwrap in the caller chain. The identical bug exists in LoadBalanceSticky::simple_increment_ptr() at load_balance_sticky.rs:82-91.
impact: Under concurrent load, the round-robin pointer can exceed the valid index range. When the returned index is used in UpstreamCandidates::get(), Vec::get() returns None. In the handler code (handler_manipulate_messages.rs:116), `upstream_chosen_opt.ok_or_else(...)` converts this to an error and returns a 500 to the client. While this doesn't panic (thanks to ok_or_else), it causes intermittent 500 errors under concurrent load, effectively a partial denial of service against the load-balanced backend.
attack_path: 1. Configure rpxy with round_robin load balancing and 2+ upstreams. 2. Send many concurrent requests to the load-balanced path. 3. Race condition between concurrent get_ptr() calls causes ptr to exceed valid range. 4. Requests that draw the out-of-range pointer receive 500 errors. 5. Under sustained concurrent load, this becomes a reliability issue.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/backend/load_balance/load_balance_main.rs:53-64 - load+branch+fetch_add is not atomic
rpxy-lib/src/backend/load_balance/load_balance_sticky.rs:82-91 - identical pattern
rpxy-lib/src/backend/upstream.rs:230-234 - upstream.get(pointer_to_upstream.ptr) can return None
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_manipulate_messages.rs:116 - ok_or_else prevents panic but returns error
remediation: Replace the non-atomic load-then-conditional-modify pattern with a single atomic operation. Use fetch_update() or a simple fetch_add with modulo: `let ptr = self.ptr.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed) % self.num_upstreams;`. This is inherently atomic and always produces a valid index.

title: Cache TOCTOU: Concurrent Requests Can Serve Partial/Corrupt Cache Data
description: The cache put() method has a race condition between the LRU metadata insertion (line 168) and the file write (line 178). The LRU entry is inserted with a CacheFileOrOnMemory::File(path) target *before* the file is actually written to disk. A concurrent get() request for the same cache key can find the LRU entry, attempt to open the file at the path, and either: (a) find no file yet (File::open fails) causing a cache eviction and error, or (b) find a partially written file and stream corrupted data to the client. The hash check in FileStoreInner::read() happens asynchronously *after* data has already started streaming to the client via the unbounded channel (lines 353-377), so corrupted/partial data reaches the client before the hash mismatch is detected.
impact: Under concurrent requests for the same cacheable resource, clients can receive truncated or corrupted response bodies. The integrity check (hash verification) runs after data has already been sent downstream, so the client receives partial data before the error is detected. This is a data integrity violation that could cause application-level failures in downstream clients.
attack_path: 1. Identify a cacheable resource on the proxy. 2. Send two near-simultaneous requests for the same resource. 3. First request triggers cache put(), which inserts LRU entry then starts async file write. 4. Second request triggers cache get(), finds the LRU entry, opens the partially-written file. 5. Second request streams partial file content to the client. 6. Hash check fails asynchronously but data is already sent.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:168 - LRU push happens before file write
rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:177-178 - file write happens after metadata insertion
rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:339-377 - read() streams data before hash verification completes
rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:362-364 - unbounded_send sends data frames before hash is checked at line 370
remediation: Write the file to a temporary path first, then atomically rename it to the final path after the write is complete and the hash is verified. Only insert the LRU entry after the file is fully written. Alternatively, use a per-key lock to serialize concurrent put/get operations for the same cache key.

title: Request Count Race Allows Exceeding max_clients via Increment-Then-Check
description: The serve_connection() method uses an increment-then-check pattern: it calls request_count.increment() which atomically increments the counter and returns the *previous* value, then checks if that previous value exceeds max_clients. However, because increment() uses fetch_add which returns the value *before* increment, and the check is `> max_clients` (not `>=`), when exactly max_clients connections arrive simultaneously, they all see a pre-increment value <= max_clients and all proceed. Additionally, because the counter is checked after incrementing, N concurrent arrivals can all increment before any checks, temporarily pushing the count to max_clients + N before decrements happen. This means the actual concurrent connection count can briefly exceed max_clients by the number of simultaneous arrivals.
impact: The max_clients limit can be transiently exceeded under burst conditions. With max_clients=512 (default), a burst of 100 simultaneous connections could temporarily push active connections to ~612. This weakens the DoS protection that max_clients is meant to provide.
attack_path: 1. Determine or guess the max_clients setting (default 512). 2. Open max_clients connections that are kept alive (e.g., slow POST bodies). 3. Rapidly open additional connections in a burst. 4. The increment-then-check pattern allows burst connections through before any decrement occurs. 5. Active connection count temporarily exceeds max_clients.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/count.rs:15-17 - increment() returns the pre-increment value via fetch_add with Relaxed ordering
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:78-81 - check is on the pre-increment value with > (not >=)
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:90-113 - spawn happens before any possible decrement
remediation: Use a check-then-increment pattern with compare_exchange in a loop: load current count, check if it's < max_clients, then CAS to increment. Only proceed if CAS succeeds. This guarantees the count never exceeds max_clients. Alternatively, use a tokio::sync::Semaphore with max_clients permits.

title: Upgraded WebSocket/Connection Streams Have No Timeout or Size Limit
description: When an HTTP connection is upgraded (e.g., WebSocket), the bidirectional copy (copy_bidirectional) runs indefinitely with no timeout, no data transfer limit, and no idle detection. The connection_handling_timeout wraps the initial serve_connection_with_upgrades future, but the upgrade spawn at handler_main.rs:222 creates a new independent task that is not bounded by any timeout. This task runs copy_bidirectional() which will keep running as long as both sides keep the connection alive, even if they exchange no data.
impact: An attacker can open WebSocket upgrade connections and keep them alive indefinitely by sending periodic WebSocket pings. Each such connection consumes a file descriptor, a tokio task, and associated memory. Since WebSocket connections also bypass max_clients (already known), this compounds the resource exhaustion. Even without bypassing max_clients, legitimate but idle WebSocket connections can hold resources indefinitely.
attack_path: 1. Establish HTTP/1.1 connection to the proxy. 2. Send an Upgrade: websocket request to a backend that supports WebSocket. 3. Complete the WebSocket handshake. 4. The proxy spawns a copy_bidirectional task with no timeout. 5. Send periodic WebSocket pings to keep the connection alive. 6. The connection persists indefinitely, consuming server resources. 7. Repeat to exhaust file descriptors or memory.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_main.rs:222-238 - spawn with no timeout wrapping copy_bidirectional
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:105-108 - connection_handling_timeout wraps serve_connection, but the upgrade task is spawned independently inside the handler
remediation: Apply a maximum lifetime timeout to the spawned upgrade task. Wrap the copy_bidirectional call in tokio::time::timeout with a configurable maximum upgrade connection duration. Also consider adding idle detection (no data transferred for N seconds).

title: No HTTP/2 Header List Size Limit Enables Header Bomb Memory Exhaustion
description: The HTTP/2 server connection builder (ConnectionBuilder) does not configure max_header_list_size(). Hyper's default for HTTP/2 max_header_list_size is 16MB (16 * 1024 * 1024 = 16777216 bytes). An attacker can send an HTTP/2 request with headers totaling up to 16MB. With max_concurrent_streams=64 (default), a single HTTP/2 connection can have 64 concurrent streams each with 16MB of headers, consuming approximately 1GB of memory per connection. With max_clients=512 connections, this scales to ~512GB theoretical maximum header memory.
impact: An attacker can exhaust server memory by sending HTTP/2 requests with very large header lists. With default settings (max_concurrent_streams=64, max_clients=512), even a modest attack of a few connections with large headers can consume gigabytes of memory, leading to OOM kills or severe performance degradation.
attack_path: 1. Establish HTTP/2 connection to the proxy. 2. Open max_concurrent_streams (64) concurrent streams. 3. On each stream, send a request with ~16MB of header data (e.g., many large custom headers). 4. Memory consumption: 64 streams * 16MB headers = ~1GB per connection. 5. Open multiple connections to amplify. 6. Server runs out of memory.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/proxy/mod.rs:30-38 - http2() builder does not call max_header_list_size()
rpxy-lib/src/constants.rs:7 - MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS is 64
rpxy-lib/src/constants.rs:6 - MAX_CLIENTS is 512
remediation: Configure a reasonable max_header_list_size on the HTTP/2 builder, e.g., `http_server.http2().max_header_list_size(64 * 1024);` (64KB is a common safe default). Also consider configuring max_send_buf_size to limit per-connection memory usage.

title: Certificate Reload Race: Stale server_crypto_map After Failed Update
description: In tls_listener_service(), the certificate reload handling (lines 284-298) replaces server_crypto_map atomically only on success. However, if the try_into() conversion at line 290 succeeds but produces a ServerCrypto with only a subset of expected server names (e.g., because one certificate file is temporarily invalid during rotation), the proxy will serve the partial set of certificates. Connections for the missing server names will fail with NoTlsServingApp errors. The old certificates are completely discarded even if only some new certificates are valid. There is no rollback mechanism.
impact: During certificate rotation, if one certificate file is temporarily in an invalid state (e.g., being written atomically but the key file is not yet updated), the proxy can load a partial certificate set. This causes TLS handshake failures for the affected server names, resulting in a partial outage. The old valid certificates are discarded with no fallback.
attack_path: 1. This is primarily a reliability issue during certificate rotation. 2. If an attacker can influence certificate file timing (e.g., by racing an ACME challenge), they could cause a window where some domains lose TLS service. 3. The server_crypto_base is rebuilt from scratch on each reload (reloader_service.rs:46-59), with individual server failures only logged and skipped (line 52). 4. The proxy replaces the entire map atomically (proxy_main.rs:298), so domains whose certs failed to load become unreachable.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:284-298 - reload replaces entire map, no rollback
rpxy-certs/src/reloader_service.rs:46-59 - failed cert reads are skipped with continue, producing partial map
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:210-212 - missing server_name returns NoTlsServingApp error
remediation: Implement a merge-on-success strategy: only replace individual server certificates that successfully loaded, keeping the previous valid certificate for any server that failed to reload. Alternatively, only apply the new certificate map if all certificates loaded successfully, falling back to the previous map otherwise.

title: FileStoreInner::cnt Can Underflow via Concurrent Remove Without Lock Coordination
description: FileStoreInner::cnt is a plain usize (not atomic), and it is decremented in remove() (line 389: self.cnt -= 1). The FileStoreInner is behind an Arc<RwLock<FileStoreInner>>, so concurrent writes should be serialized. However, there is a path where remove() is called from within read() (line 373), which holds only a read lock via the clone of self_clone. This clone has its own copy of cnt (FileStoreInner derives Clone), so the decrement on the clone does not affect the original. Additionally, the cnt on the original can underflow: if evict() is called on a path that was already removed by the hash-mismatch path in read(), the second remove will fail with FailedToRemoveCacheFile (file already deleted), but if the file happened to be recreated by a concurrent put, the cnt will be decremented again, going below the actual count.
impact: The file cache count (cnt) becomes inconsistent with the actual number of cached files. This is a bookkeeping error that could lead to incorrect cache statistics. Since cnt is only used for count() which feeds debug logging, the operational impact is low, but it indicates broader synchronization issues in the cache layer.
attack_path: 1. Send requests to create file cache entries. 2. Send concurrent requests that trigger hash mismatches in read() (via the file corruption race in finding #2). 3. The cloned self_clone's remove() modifies a copy of cnt, not the original. 4. Concurrent evict() from the stale-cache path also tries to remove the same file. 5. cnt becomes inconsistent.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:349 - self.clone() inside read() creates a copy of cnt
rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:373 - self_clone.remove() modifies the clone's cnt, not the locked original
rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:385-393 - remove decrements cnt unconditionally
rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:295 - derives Clone for FileStoreInner
remediation: Use AtomicUsize for the file count or avoid cloning FileStoreInner. The read-path hash-mismatch removal should signal the outer FileStore to perform the eviction under the write lock, rather than trying to modify state through a cloned copy.

title: No Connection Timeout on Cleartext HTTP Accept Loop Enables Slow Connection Exhaustion
description: The start_without_tls() method (lines 117-129) accepts TCP connections and immediately passes them to serve_connection(). There is no connection_handling_timeout applied when connection_handling_timeout is None (the default). The hyper server has header_read_timeout set to proxy_idle_timeout (default 20 seconds), which helps, but once headers are read, if the upstream backend is slow to respond or the client is slow to read the response, the connection can be held open indefinitely. The default connection_handling_timeout is None, meaning there is no overall time limit on connection handling.
impact: Without connection_handling_timeout configured (which is the default), connections that pass the header read phase can be held open indefinitely. An attacker can send a valid request header, then read the response extremely slowly (1 byte per second), holding the connection and its associated resources for hours. With max_clients=512, this requires only 512 such connections to exhaust the connection limit.
attack_path: 1. Open a TCP connection to the HTTP cleartext port. 2. Send valid HTTP/1.1 request headers within the 20-second header_read_timeout. 3. The proxy forwards the request to the upstream and begins sending the response. 4. Read the response at 1 byte per second (slow-read attack). 5. The connection is held open indefinitely since connection_handling_timeout defaults to None. 6. Repeat 512 times to exhaust max_clients. 7. All subsequent legitimate connections are rejected.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/globals.rs:104 - connection_handling_timeout defaults to None
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:105-108 - timeout only applied if connection_handling_timeout is Some
rpxy-lib/src/proxy/proxy_main.rs:107 - without timeout, fut.await runs indefinitely
rpxy-lib/src/constants.rs:6 - MAX_CLIENTS is only 512
remediation: Set a default connection_handling_timeout (e.g., 300 seconds) rather than defaulting to None. This ensures connections cannot be held open indefinitely even if the administrator doesn't explicitly configure a timeout.

title: SNI Consistency Check Bypass When sni_consistency is Disabled Enables Backend Confusion
description: When sni_consistency is disabled (configurable, though default is true), the proxy routes requests based on the Host header alone, ignoring the TLS SNI. An attacker can establish a TLS connection using SNI for domain A (which they control or have a certificate for), then send HTTP requests with Host: domain-B headers. The proxy will route these requests to domain-B's backend, but the TLS certificate presented to the client was for domain-A. This is a form of backend confusion where the attacker can access backends they shouldn't be able to reach, or where the backend sees traffic it believes came via its own domain.
impact: When sni_consistency is disabled, an attacker can route requests to any configured backend by manipulating the Host header, regardless of which TLS certificate was used for the connection. This can be used to bypass per-domain access controls if the backend relies on the proxy's TLS termination for domain validation.
attack_path: 1. Ensure target proxy has sni_consistency disabled (not default, but configurable). 2. Establish TLS connection with SNI set to a domain the attacker controls. 3. Send HTTP requests with Host header set to a different domain configured on the proxy. 4. The proxy routes the request to the second domain's backend. 5. The backend sees a valid request that appears to come from its domain.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_main.rs:101-105 - SNI check only when sni_consistency is true
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_main.rs:94-97 - server_name derived from Host header only
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/handler_main.rs:107-116 - routing uses Host-derived server_name
remediation: Consider making sni_consistency a mandatory check that cannot be disabled, or at minimum log a security warning when it is disabled. When sni_consistency is disabled, consider limiting request routing to only the backend that matches the TLS SNI, using the Host header only as a secondary hint.

title: X-Forwarded-For Header Spoofing via Append Semantics
description: The add_forwarding_header() function uses append_header_entry_with_comma() for X-Forwarded-For, which appends the client address to any existing X-Forwarded-For header. An external attacker can set an arbitrary X-Forwarded-For header in their request (e.g., 'X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1'), and the proxy will append the real client IP, resulting in 'X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1, <real-ip>'. Backends that use the *first* value of X-Forwarded-For (a common pattern) will see the spoofed IP. While add_header_entry_overwrite_if_exist is used for x-real-ip (line 224), correctly overwriting the attacker's value, the X-Forwarded-For append behavior is the standard for multi-hop proxies. However, this proxy is typically the first hop from the internet, meaning it should strip or replace any incoming X-Forwarded-For header from untrusted clients.
impact: Backend applications that trust the first entry in X-Forwarded-For for IP-based access control, rate limiting, or logging will use the attacker-controlled spoofed IP instead of the real client IP. This can bypass IP-based restrictions on backend applications.
attack_path: 1. Send a request with header 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1' to the proxy. 2. The proxy appends the real client IP: 'X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1, <real-ip>'. 3. Backend receives the request with spoofed first entry. 4. If backend uses the first X-Forwarded-For value for access control, attacker bypasses IP restrictions.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/utils_headers.rs:208 - append_header_entry_with_comma for x-forwarded-for
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/utils_headers.rs:128-144 - append_header_entry_with_comma preserves existing values
rpxy-lib/src/message_handler/utils_headers.rs:85-87 - remove_hop_header does not include x-forwarded-for
remediation: When the proxy is the edge/first-hop proxy (the common deployment), it should replace (not append to) the X-Forwarded-For header with the actual client IP. Add a configuration option to control whether the proxy operates in 'edge' mode (replace X-Forwarded-For) or 'intermediate' mode (append to X-Forwarded-For).

title: Unbounded BytesMut Accumulation in Cache Put Path Enables Memory Exhaustion
description: In the cache put() method's spawned task, response body frames are accumulated into a BytesMut buffer (line 110: let mut buf = BytesMut::new()) up to max_each_size (default 65535 bytes). However, the size check (line 130) only triggers after the current frame has already been added to buf (line 141). If a single frame exceeds max_each_size, the buffer will contain the entire oversized frame before the check triggers. More importantly, this buffering happens in a spawned task per cacheable response, and there is no global limit on how many cache-put operations can run concurrently. If many different cacheable URIs are requested simultaneously, each spawns a task that buffers up to max_each_size bytes, potentially consuming significant memory.
impact: With many concurrent requests for different cacheable resources, the proxy can accumulate significant memory in in-flight cache put operations. Each operation buffers up to 65535 bytes (default max_each_size). With 512 concurrent connections, this is ~32MB, which is manageable. However, if max_each_size is configured to a larger value, this scales linearly.
attack_path: 1. Identify or create many distinct cacheable resources on backends. 2. Send concurrent requests for different cacheable resources. 3. Each request spawns a cache-put task that buffers the response body. 4. Memory consumption: num_concurrent * max_each_size bytes. 5. With elevated max_each_size settings, this can be significant.
evidence: rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:108-182 - spawned task per cacheable response
rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:110 - BytesMut::new() with no pre-allocation limit
rpxy-lib/src/forwarder/cache/cache_main.rs:141 - buf.extend before size check on next iteration
remediation: Limit the number of concurrent cache-put operations using a semaphore. Consider streaming cache writes to disk instead of buffering the entire body in memory before writing.
